newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS - Worst may be over for CHH - analysts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Worst may be over for CHH - analysts.

text.p: A commodities price slump reduced Carter Holt Harvey Ltd's annual profit by 45 percent but analysts said on Tuesday the worst may be over for the forest products company.
CHH earlier reported a net profit of NZ$251 million, an improvement on market expectations of NZ$235-240 million, but down from last year's record profit of $453 million.
The decline was caused entirely by a price slump in almost all the areas CHH is involved in.
Analysts said a higher-than-expected monetary adjustment between the Chilean peso and the New Zealand dollar had put forecasts out of sync.

CHH has an indirect holding of just over 30 percent in Chilean forestry, fishing and petroleum company Copec. Earnings from associated companies -- mostly Copec -- fell to NZ$75 million from $126 million.
Analysts agreed with CHH chief executive John Faraci's assessment that the outlook for pulp and paper may be looking up and that the chances of another "double dip" were unlikely.

"I believe the fundamentals now are better for a pulp price increase that will stick, relative to fundamentals in the third quarter of last year when prices didn't stick," Faraci told a briefing of analysts and journalists.

In the U.S., pulp prices have recovered to levels similar to those of the third and fourth quarters of calendar 1996 at US$580 per tonne. Faraci expected better prices to flow through to earnings in June, July and August.
But he said that while inventory levels had eased somewhat, they were still too high.
Cavill White analyst John Cairns said CHH was probably past its cyclical low in terms of earnings, but the question was how quickly it would recover.
"The immediate outlook is that they will not recover that quickly," he said.
Steve Cozens at First NZ Capital said pulp and paper demand appeared relatively robust, but there was still excess supply.
Cozens said he agreed that further increases in pulp prices were likely in the short term, but the market would get tougher later in the year.
However, it did appear the worst was over for CHH, which is just over half-owned by International Paper.

Cairns said the earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) of CHH's wood and forest products division, of NZ$147 million (vs $221 million), were in line with expectations. He said pulp and paper's EBIT of NZ$111 million ($178 million) was creditable.
Packaging's EBIT fell to NZ$41 million against $55 million. Despite increased volume, the division's margins had been squeezed by competition.
EBIT from building products was depressed at NZ$15 million from $36 million, but much of that was due to writeoffs.
Overall, CHH said it gleaned NZ$70 million through cost cutting, productivity gains and higher volumes.

Analysts did not expect much share price reaction to the result, as cyclical issues had already been priced in. By 1.15 p.m. (0115 GMT), CHH was up four cents at NZ$3.27, off its earlier peak of $3.29.
-- Wellington Newsroom (64-4-4734746)
